scenes.narration: You open your phone to check one thing. Twenty minutes later, you're still scrolling.
scenes.art: a young adult lying in bed at night, face lit by a glowing phone, an endless stream of colorful cards flowing out of the phone, a wall clock showing late time

scenes.narration: It's not just weak willpower. A few things are working on you.
scenes.art: a tiny young adult standing in front of a giant smartphone with cartoon hooks and magnets reaching out of the screen toward them

scenes.narration: One: habit. A typical phone check lasts under thirty seconds, and it's triggered by the same moments, like boredom or a commute.
scenes.art: a young adult on a bus commute checking a phone out of boredom, small thought bubble with a yawning face, calm teal city outside the window

scenes.narration: Two: rewards. Most posts are meh, then one is great. Studies of social media find our behavior follows the rules of reward learning.
scenes.art: a cute cartoon brain character pulling a slot machine lever, the slot reels showing hearts, thumbs up and laughing faces, notification bubbles floating

scenes.narration: So it's not simply a dopamine addiction. It's learning, habit and design working together.
scenes.art: three glowing interlocking gears labeled only with simple icons: a loop arrow, a star, and a phone screen, floating in space

scenes.narration: Three: no stopping point. A book has chapters. A feed has no last page.
scenes.art: a split image: on the left an open book with a clear final page and a bookmark, on the right a phone feed stretching endlessly upward into the stars

scenes.narration: And alerts keep pulling you back. In one study, just getting a notification, without even checking it, made people miss more on a focus task.
scenes.art: a young adult trying to focus on homework at a desk while a phone buzzes with a glowing notification bubble, their attention drawn by a dotted line to the phone

scenes.narration: So try this: batch your notifications. In one trial, getting them just three times a day lowered stress and helped people feel more focused.
scenes.art: a calm young adult relaxing with tea while a phone rests face down, three small neat envelopes arriving at a clock showing morning, noon and evening
scenes.cite: Fitz et al., Computers in Human Behavior 2019

scenes.narration: Now be honest. How many times have you checked your phone today?

post.title: Why you can't stop scrolling (it's not just dopamine) 📱
post.description:
Habit, reward learning and feeds with no last page. Plus one simple fix that actually has evidence behind it.

Sources:
Oulasvirta et al. (2012) Personal and Ubiquitous Computing
Lindström et al. (2021) Nature Communications
Stothart et al. (2015) J Exp Psychol: Human Perception and Performance
Fitz et al. (2019) Computers in Human Behavior
